questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

content.text:
The ESP32 work is in two separate pieces that aren't connected yet: firmware that records audio, and a pipeline that exports a model for the chip. The firmware doesn't run the model.

## 1. Firmware: `firmware/esp32-sense/` (one commit, `a06681d`, merged into main)

This is for the Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 Sense, and it only records. It copies the Pi's ring-buffer recording so the board can eventually replace the Pi Zero W.

**Done:**
- **Triggered recording:** it listens on an MQTT topic (default `doorbell/trigger`), and any message saves a clip. The clip has 3 s of audio from before the trigger (kept in a ring buffer in PSRAM) plus 6 s after. It's written to `/recordings/doorbell_manual_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.wav` on the SD card, at 16 kHz / mono / int16 from the onboard mic.
- **Safe file writes:** each clip is written to a `.tmp` file first and renamed when complete, so the uploader never sees a half-written file.
- **Daily upload:** around 3 am local time (from NTP and a timezone string), and once right after boot, it sends every `.wav` to MinIO at `esp32-recordings/<DEVICE_ID>/<file>`. Each file is deleted once its upload succeeds.
- **Upload signing:** S3 request signing is hand-written in `lib/sigv4core/` and has no Arduino dependency. It has a unit test against AWS's published example request (`./build.sh test -e native`), which runs without the board.
- **Plumbing:** WiFi reconnects on its own, MQTT supports optional auth, and NTP re-syncs every 6 h. Networking runs on core 0 and audio on core 1. Secrets are compiled in from a git-ignored `.env.esp32` through `build.sh`.
- According to the commit message, the whole firmware compiles for the real board.

**Not done (by design, per the README):** no detection, no on-device ML, no TLS, no OTA updates, no camera, no GPIO button, no check for SD free space.

**Not verified:** nothing in the repo shows the end-to-end checklist in the README was ever run on a board: trigger → WAV on the SD card → object in MinIO. PlatformIO (`pio`) isn't installed on this machine, so I couldn't run the unit test or a build.

## 2. Model export for the chip (the ML pipeline)
- `params.yaml` defaults to a log-mel layout sized for ESP32-S3 inference.
- `quantize_model` exports an int8 TFLite model plus a C array (`doorbell_model_data.cc`, variable `g_doorbell_model_data`). `evaluate_quantized` then checks the int8 model hasn't drifted too far from the float version.
- **Not wired up:** the firmware doesn't include that C array, has no TFLite Micro dependency, and has no log-mel feature code. Running the detector on the chip is the big missing step.

## Things I noticed while reading
- **A trigger during an upload can stall recording.** The upload holds the SD-card lock for the whole pass, across every file (`upload_scheduler.cpp:22`). If a trigger fires during that pass, the audio loop blocks when it tries to save the clip. While it waits, it stops reading the mic and stops filling the ring buffer. The comment in `audio_capture.cpp` says the lock is released "in bounded time", but a long pass can take minutes.
- **A failed upload waits until the next day.** `g_uploaded_today` is set to true even when uploads fail. Failed files are only retried the next day or after a reboot.
- **Triggers during a recording queue one extra clip.** A trigger arriving while a clip is being recorded stays pending, and another clip starts as soon as the current one finishes.

A sensible next step is to run the hardware checklist in the README. After that, either fix the upload-lock issue or start the on-device inference work (TFLite Micro, a log-mel front end matching `features.py`, and the exported C array).

content.text:
**To compile, you only need PlatformIO.** Everything else it needs is already here: Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL2, Python 3.11, `uv`, and gcc/g++/make. `pio` itself is missing.

```bash
uv tool install platformio        # the README's suggestion; nothing else on the system changes
```

On the first `./build.sh run`, PlatformIO downloads the rest itself: the espressif32@6.9.0 platform, the Xtensa ESP32-S3 compiler, the Arduino core, PubSubClient and esptool. That's a few hundred MB into `~/.platformio`, so expect the first build to be slow. The host-side unit tests (`./build.sh test -e native`) use the gcc/g++ you already have.

You also need to create `.env.esp32` from the example file before building. Without it, `build.sh` only prints a warning, and the build flags get empty strings, so it compiles a binary with empty credentials.

**To flash, the board is plugged in, but WSL can't see it yet.** Windows shows it as `303a:1001 USB JTAG/serial debug unit (COM35)` on bus ID **8-3**, state *Not shared*. WSL has no `/dev/ttyACM*` device. `usbipd-win` 5.3.0 is already installed on the Windows side, so you don't need to install anything else. These steps are missing:

1. **Share the board and attach it to WSL.** Run this once in an admin PowerShell:
   ```powershell
   usbipd bind --busid 8-3
   ```
   Then run this every time you plug the board in (it can be a normal shell):
   ```powershell
   usbipd attach --wsl --busid 8-3
   ```
   After that it should show up in WSL as `/dev/ttyACM0`.
2. **Give yourself access to the serial port.** Your account isn't in the `dialout` group, so you'd get permission denied on the port:
   ```bash
   sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER    # then restart WSL: `wsl --shutdown` from Windows
   ```
   PlatformIO's udev rules are optional here. The ESP32-S3's built-in USB interface works with the kernel's standard driver, and joining `dialout` is enough.
3. **Flash:** `./build.sh run -t upload`, then `./build.sh device monitor`.

Some notes:
- The bus ID can change if you use a different USB port.
- The S3 re-enumerates when it resets into the bootloader, so an upload can fail halfway because WSL loses the device. If that happens, run `usbipd attach --wsl --busid 8-3 --auto-attach` so it reattaches automatically. Or put the board into download mode by hand: hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT.
- Another option skips usbipd completely: build in WSL, then flash from Windows with esptool against `COM35`. The usbipd route keeps everything inside `./build.sh`, though, so I'd use that.

I haven't installed or changed anything. If you want, I can run the `uv tool install platformio` step and a first compile now.

content.text:
I flashed the board successfully, but it stops at boot: **it can't read the SD card**, so none of the recording or upload code runs.

```
rst:0x15 (USB_UART_CHIP_RESET),boot:0x8 (SPI_FAST_FLASH_BOOT)
[   193][E][sd_diskio.cpp:806] sdcard_mount(): f_mount failed: (13) There is no valid FAT volume
FATAL: SD card init failed
```

**What's working:** the build with your real config, the flash (825 KB written and checked), the reset, and the board booting into the firmware. `setup()` treats a failed SD mount as fatal and halts there, so WiFi, MQTT and the mic are never started.

**The cause:** a card is inserted and responding, but it isn't formatted as FAT. Error 13 means no FAT volume was found; an empty slot gives a different error. This is usually one of two things:
- **The card is exFAT.** Cards over 32 GB (SDXC) come formatted that way, and this Arduino version's SD library only reads FAT16/FAT32.
- **The card is blank or has another filesystem**, such as ext4 or a Pi image.

**Fix:** reformat the card as **FAT32** with an MBR partition table and put it back in the board.
- On Windows, the built-in formatter won't offer FAT32 for cards over 32 GB. Use the SD Association's "SD Card Formatter" for cards up to 32 GB, or a tool like `guiformat` for bigger ones.
- On Linux, run `sudo mkfs.vfat -F 32 /dev/sdX1`.
- Reformatting erases the card.

After the card is reinserted, tell me and I'll reset the board and read the log again. I'd expect to see WiFi connect, MQTT subscribe, and NTP sync. Once those show up, the next check is `mosquitto_pub -t doorbell/trigger -m x` to record a first clip.

content.text:
It isn't working yet: the board still stops at boot with the same SD card error. The flash itself is now fine.

- **Reattach:** the board was still shared in usbipd but not attached. I attached it from WSL (`usbipd attach --wsl --busid 8-3`), and `/dev/ttyACM0` came back.
- **Reflash:** my first try failed with `No serial data received`. That was my mistake: I started reading the boot log at the same time, and both fought over the serial port. Run on its own, the flash succeeded and verified.
- **Boot log** after a reset:
  ```
  [   193][E][sd_diskio.cpp:806] sdcard_mount(): f_mount failed: (13) There is no valid FAT volume
  FATAL: SD card init failed
  ```

So the board still finds no FAT volume on the card, and it halts before WiFi, MQTT or the mic start. Reflashing couldn't have fixed this, since the firmware didn't change. If you did reformat the card, one of these is the likely cause:

1. **It was formatted exFAT, not FAT32.** Windows' built-in formatter does this silently for cards over 32 GB.
2. **The partition table is GPT, not MBR.** The FAT library in this Arduino core only reads MBR, so a FAT32 card with a GPT table looks empty. You can see which one it has in Windows Disk Management (Disk properties → Volumes → "Partition style").
3. **The card went back into the Pi or a reader** rather than the XIAO. The slot is on the camera/Sense expansion board, and that board has to be clipped firmly onto the XIAO.

Did you reformat the card, and how big is it? If you put it in a reader attached to this machine, I can check its partition table and filesystem directly. I'd need to attach the reader to WSL with usbipd first. Any fix that means reformatting the card erases it, so I'd ask you before running anything like that.

content.text:
"ext32" isn't a real filesystem, so I can't tell which one you picked. Windows offers exactly three for SD cards, and only one works with the board:

| Windows option | Works with the ESP32? |
|---|---|
| **FAT32** | ✅ yes, this is the one you need |
| exFAT | ❌ no, gives exactly the `no valid FAT volume` error you're seeing |
| NTFS | ❌ no, same error |

The error means the board can read the card but can't find a FAT volume on it. That points to exFAT or NTFS, not a bad contact. A 16 GB card is fine for FAT32; Windows only hides that option on cards over 32 GB.

**To fix it:**
1. Put the card back in the Windows reader.
2. Open Explorer, right-click the drive and choose **Format…**.
3. Set **File system** to **FAT32**, allocation unit to the default, and leave **Quick Format** on.
4. Eject it properly, put it back in the XIAO's Sense board, and tell me. I'll reset the board and read the boot log.

**If you want to know what it is right now:** while the card is in the Windows reader, I can check it from here without changing anything. I'd run `powershell.exe Get-Volume` for the filesystem and `Get-Disk` for the partition style. That also rules out the GPT partition table problem from before. You don't need to attach anything to WSL for this.

content.text:
The board is flashed and booting cleanly past the SD card, but I could only confirm half of it: I can't tell from here whether WiFi and MQTT are working.

**What I did:**
- Reattached the board to WSL (bus 8-3 → `/dev/ttyACM0`).
- Flashed it. The normal `./build.sh run -t upload` failed three times with `No serial data received`, every time just after esptool raised the connection speed. Flashing esptool directly at 115200 with `--no-stub` worked, and every part verified. Your MBR reformat fixed the SD error.

**Boot log** after a reset, captured for 60 s:
```
rst:0x15 (USB_UART_CHIP_RESET),boot:0x8 (SPI_FAST_FLASH_BOOT)
...
Doorbell recorder ready.
```
"Doorbell recorder ready." is printed only after everything in `setup()` has succeeded. So these are confirmed working:
- The SD card mounts.
- The audio buffers are allocated in PSRAM.
- The microphone starts.
- The networking task has started.

**Not confirmed: WiFi, MQTT, NTP, recording and upload.** The networking, recording and upload code doesn't print anything at all. A board that joined WiFi and one that's stuck retrying the password produce the same serial output, so I can't tell them apart from here.

**You can test it yourself now:**
1. Publish a trigger: `mosquitto_pub -h <broker> -t doorbell/trigger -m x`.
2. Wait at least 9 s (the clip length), then reset the board. On boot, once NTP has synced, it uploads anything already on the SD card, so you don't have to wait for 3 am.
3. Look in MinIO under `doorbell-detector/esp32-recordings/<DEVICE_ID>/` for a `doorbell_manual_*.wav`. If it's there, the whole chain works: WiFi, MQTT, recording, SD, NTP and the signed upload.

I can't do these steps myself: I don't know the broker address, and the root `.env` with the MinIO keys is blocked to me.

**My suggestion:** I could add one-line serial messages for WiFi connect (with the IP), MQTT connect and subscribe, NTP sync, each saved clip, and each upload result with its HTTP status. Then I could check everything from the boot log myself, and future problems would be visible on the serial port. Separately, I could set `upload_speed = 115200` in `platformio.ini` (or make `--no-stub` the default) so `./build.sh run -t upload` works over usbipd again. Want me to make those changes?

content.text:
The serial log doesn't show whether your recording was saved, and opening the port reset the board, even though I'd set the reset lines so it shouldn't. Any recording that was still capturing at that moment was lost; one already saved is still on the SD card. The reboot did surface a real network error, though.

**What the log shows after that reboot:**
```
Doorbell recorder ready.
[  1510][E][WiFiClient.cpp:429] write(): fail on fd 48, errno: 104, "Connection reset by peer"
```

- **WiFi works.** Error 104 means a server accepted a connection from the board and then dropped it. That can only happen if the board is on the network and the server address is reachable.
- **But a server cut the board off about 1.5 s after boot.** Only two things connect out that early: the MQTT client, or the start-up upload of any clips already on the card. The firmware doesn't log which one it was.
- **My main suspect is MQTT over TLS.** The project notes say both Pi scripts connect to the broker with TLS (`ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS`), but this firmware only speaks plain MQTT. If `ESP32_MQTT_PORT` in `.env.esp32` points at the broker's TLS port, or the broker only accepts TLS, it would reset the connection exactly like this. In that case MQTT never connects, triggers never reach the board, and no recording was made.
- **The other suspect is MinIO behind HTTPS.** If your recording did get saved, the reboot started an upload. That would be dropped the same way if `ESP32_MINIO_ENDPOINT` points at an HTTPS front end, since the firmware only speaks plain HTTP.

**You can sort this out quickly:**
1. Check which port `ESP32_MQTT_PORT` is set to, and whether that broker port accepts plain MQTT. Port 1883 is normally plain and 8883 normally TLS; whatever the Pi uses is probably TLS.
2. Look in the broker's log for a client called `esp32-sense-<DEVICE_ID>`. A TLS handshake error or a "socket error" for it there settles the question.
3. Look in MinIO under `esp32-recordings/<DEVICE_ID>/` in case a clip did make it.

**What I'd do next:** add the serial messages I suggested earlier, covering WiFi and the board's IP, MQTT connect with its error code, NTP sync, each saved clip, and each upload with its HTTP status. A connection drop like this one then shows exactly which connection failed. Since opening the port reboots the board anyway, a full boot log tells us everything. I can make that change and flash it now. If it does turn out to be TLS, the fix is either a plain listener on the broker for the LAN or adding TLS to the firmware's MQTT client.

content.text:
The broker log shows MQTT is fine. "Session taken over" is just the board reconnecting after my accidental reset. The new connection at 09:38:31 came from 192.168.178.167 and authenticated as `mic`. So WiFi, MQTT auth and the subscription all work, which rules out TLS.

That leaves the start-up upload as the likely source of the reset. It only runs when a clip is on the SD card, so your trigger probably did record something, and then MinIO dropped the upload partway through. The usual pattern: MinIO rejects the request as soon as it reads the headers (bad signature, wrong region, missing bucket) and closes the socket while the board is still sending the WAV body. The board then sees exactly `Connection reset by peer` on `write()`, and never gets to read MinIO's error reply.

To see that reply I need logging, so I'll add it now, flash, and reboot. The reboot reruns the start-up upload, so the log should show MinIO's actual response.

content.text:
Recording works end to end, but the upload to MinIO fails, and I can't see why from the board.

The board found 4 clips on the SD card, so your trigger and the earlier ones were all saved:
```
ntp: synced, local time 2026-10-01 07:52:19
wifi: connected, ip 192.168.178.167
upload: pass started, 4 file(s)
[  1030][E][WiFiClient.cpp:429] write(): fail on fd 48, errno: 104, "Connection reset by peer"
upload: esp32-recordings/xiao-sense-01/doorbell_manual_20261001_072902.wav -> failed (-3 send payload failed)
... same for _074154, _074638, _074845 ...
mqtt: connected, subscribe doorbell/trigger ok
```

**Working:** WiFi, NTP, MQTT connect and subscribe, triggers, recording, and saving to the SD card. Failed uploads leave the files on the card, and every boot retries them, so nothing is lost.

**The upload problem:** for every file, MinIO accepts the connection, takes the request headers, and drops the connection while the board is still sending the audio. That almost always means MinIO rejected the request from its headers alone: bad signature, wrong region, unknown key, missing bucket, or a redirect. It sends a short error reply and closes. The board's HTTP library gives up as soon as the send fails, so it never reads that reply. I can't see the reason from the board's side yet.

**Quickest way to see MinIO's reason:** run this on your machine, then tell me and I'll reset the board so it retries the 4 uploads:
```bash
mc admin trace --errors <your-minio-alias>     # or: mc admin trace -v <alias>
```
It prints the rejected PUTs with MinIO's error code, such as `SignatureDoesNotMatch`, `InvalidAccessKeyId`, `AuthorizationHeaderMalformed` (wrong region) or `NoSuchBucket`. That tells us exactly what to fix. If you'd rather not, I can make the board read MinIO's reply even when the connection is dropped. That's more code, though, and the trace is faster.

Things I'm checking against MinIO's answer:
- **Region:** MinIO's default is `us-east-1`. If `ESP32_MINIO_REGION` is set to anything else, MinIO rejects every request.
- **Endpoint format:** it must be `host:port` exactly as the Pi's `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` has it, minus `http://`. The board signs that exact string as the `Host` header.

**A second bug, separate from the upload:** the timezone isn't applied. The board reports `07:52` local time, but your broker logs `09:38`, so the board is running on UTC. The files are named in UTC, and the daily upload would run at 03:00 UTC (05:00 your time) instead of 03:00 local. Check `ESP32_TZ` in `.env.esp32`: it should be a POSIX TZ string like `CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3`, not `Europe/Berlin`, which the board doesn't understand and silently treats as UTC.

The logging changes (5 files under `firmware/esp32-sense/src/`) aren't committed, and `./build.sh run -t upload` still uses the speed that fails over usbipd. I flashed directly at 115200 with `--no-stub`.

The board now works end to end: it records on an MQTT trigger, saves the clip to the SD card, and uploads it to MinIO.

The upload failed because your bucket setting is `doorbell-detector/raw`. The firmware turned that `/` into `%2F`, so MinIO checked the signature against a different path than the one the board signed. I changed one line in `src/s3_uploader.cpp` so the `/` is kept as a path separator. The bucket is now `doorbell-detector` and the files go under `raw/`.

**After the fix:**
- The boot right after flashing uploaded 3 of the 4 clips. On the next boot the last one went up with `HTTP 200`.
- A third boot found `0 file(s)` on the card, so all 4 recordings are in MinIO under `doorbell-detector/raw/esp32-recordings/xiao-sense-01/`. Your trace should show four `200 OK` PutObjects.
- That boot also showed MQTT connecting and subscribing to `doorbell/trigger`.

**Still open:**
1. **The timezone is still UTC.** The board's local time read 09:39 while your clock showed about 11:38 CEST. So file names are in UTC, and the daily upload runs at 05:00 your time instead of 03:00. Check `ESP32_TZ` in `.env.esp32`; it should look like `CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3`. The upload signatures always use UTC, so this doesn't affect them.

3. **`./build.sh run -t upload` still fails over usbipd.** I flashed with esptool directly at 115200 and `--no-stub` each time. I can put that into `platformio.ini` so the normal command works.
4. **Nothing is committed yet.** That's the serial logging (5 files under `firmware/esp32-sense/src/`) and the bucket fix.
